The excursion begins in Montevideo and follows the coast to Piriápolis, one of Uruguay’s oldest resorts. You will travel along the Rambla Costanera, see the historic Gran Hotel Argentino and ascend San Antonio Hill for a panorama of the city and coastline.

The next stop is Punta Ballena, home to Casapueblo, the house and art gallery of artist Carlos Páez Vilaró.

The route then continues to Punta del Este, passing through residential neighborhoods with mansions and gardens and along the waterfront lined with the resort’s well-known hotels.

On the return to Montevideo, you may choose to stop at the Alta Bagüena winery. Wine tasting is charged separately.

The excursion day, including transfers, lasts 11 hours.

Driving time from Quito to Quilotoa is 3.5 hours; from Quilotoa to Baños it is 3.5 hours.

Excursion altitude: 3,900 m. Overnight altitude: 1,800 m.

Average temperature during the excursion: +10°C.

We depart Quito along the Pan-American Highway toward a rose plantation in the Cotopaxi Valley. There, we will see roses of different colors and sizes that Ecuador exports around the world. We will observe cutting, sorting and packing, processes that demonstrate the high quality of the exported flowers.

Please note: the plantation is not visited on weekends or public holidays!

The journey continues toward Quilotoa Volcano. On the way, we visit an artisan workshop in the village of Tigua, birthplace of the “naïve” painting style depicting Andean landscapes of Ecuador on sheepskin.

We then travel west toward Ecuador’s Central Andes, following the route known as the “Pujilí Road” and passing through the village of Quilotoa.

At Quilotoa Crater, we will visit a viewpoint overlooking the crater lake and may walk through an Indigenous community.

If the whole group wishes, we may descend on foot to the lakeshore, go kayaking and return on mules. Kayaking and mule rides are not included in the price.

Mule transport uphill is an informal service offered by local residents, approximately until 15:00.

Stops: rose plantation, viewpoints, Indigenous painting gallery and crater lake.

The journey then continues to Baños.

Quito lies at an altitude of 2,800 m. During the excursion, you will see panoramas of the city, churches, domes and roofs of the historic center, and learn about the capital’s colonial art, architecture, culture, legends and traditions. The city was founded in the sixteenth century on the ruins of an Inca city. Despite the 1917 earthquake, its historic center has remained largely unchanged.

The architecture and interiors of old Quito reflect the Quito School of Art, which combined Spanish, Italian, Moorish, Flemish and Indigenous traditions. Local artisans worked in stone and wood to create religious artworks. After roughly an hour and a half walking through the Old Town, it becomes clearer why Quito was among the first cities in the world inscribed on UNESCO’s cultural heritage list.

The city’s name is linked to the Quitu people, who lived in the region before the Spanish conquest. In 1533, the city came under the control of Sebastián de Belalcázar, and in 1541 it received the status of a Spanish city and the full name San Francisco de Quito. The Franciscan order was among the first to settle here and began building a monastery that became a center of education, painting and sculpture.

The route passes through Plaza Grande, home to the Cathedral, Presidential Palace, Archbishop’s Palace and City Hall. The program also includes a Jesuit church with an elaborately carved façade and the Church of San Francisco.

From the Panecillo viewpoint, you can see the city and the statue of the winged Virgin Mary, Quito’s patroness.

After exploring the historic center, we continue to the “Middle of the World.” There are two sites here associated with the equator line.

The first is Mitad del Mundo, a tourist complex with a monument commemorating the geodetic expedition of 1736. The complex is located in the parish of San Antonio in the Quito Metropolitan District and belongs to the prefecture of Pichincha Province. Construction of a headquarters for the Union of South American Nations was also planned on the complex grounds.

The 30 m monument was erected between 1979 and 1982. A line extends from its center marking what was long believed to be the equator. GPS later established that the actual equator lies approximately 240 m farther north.

The second location is the Intiñan Museum. It presents demonstrations associated with the equator line, explains the cultures of Indigenous peoples of South America and displays traditional homes and household objects.

After the excursion, you return to the hotel.

The excursion day, including transfers, lasts 8 hours.

Altitude: 2,800 m.

Average temperature: +20°C by day and +10°C at night.

During the sightseeing excursion through Quito, you will enjoy captivating panoramas, churches, domes and rooftops that form part of the city’s historic heritage, while learning about colonial art, architecture, culture, legends and traditions.

Quito, Ecuador’s capital, was founded in the sixteenth century on the ruins of an Inca city and stands at an altitude of 2,800 m. Colonial architecture survives in the historic center. Its buildings and rich interiors exemplify the Quito School of Art, a fusion of Spanish, Italian, Moorish, Flemish and Indigenous artistic traditions. Artists of this school worked in stone and wood to give form to important religious events. After an hour-and-a-half walking tour of the Old Town, you will understand why Quito’s historic center entered the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Quito takes its name from the Quitu people, who inhabited the region long before the Spanish conquest. In 1533, Sebastián de Belalcázar took control of the city, which had previously been a capital of the Inca Empire, and in 1541 it was granted the status of a Spanish city. Its full name is San Francisco de Quito. The city remained the capital of the state of Quito until the end of Spanish colonial rule.

The Franciscan order was the first religious order established in Quito. The Franciscans immediately began building a monastery that became a center of education and art, with its own schools of painting and sculpture.

The country’s principal buildings surround Plaza Grande, the main square: the Cathedral, Presidential Palace, Archbishop’s Palace and City Hall. We will visit the city’s finest example of colonial art, a Jesuit church whose façade is covered in intricate carvings.

We will also visit the Gothic Basilica del Voto Nacional:

The religious building was designed by a French architect inspired by Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. The Basilica of the National Vow is considered the country’s most representative work of Neo-Gothic architecture and one of the most notable in Latin America.

Founded in the nineteenth century and regarded as unfinished, the basilica has gargoyles on its façade as well as sculptures of animals endemic to the country and region, including caimans, turtles, boobies, monkeys and others.

This religious building measures 140 m in length, 35 m in width, and its central nave is 30 m high.

The two front towers rise to 115 m. The basilica is one of the tallest buildings in the city!

Quito is a capital full of contrasts, which you can appreciate while visiting the old city and its newer districts.

A beautiful view over the entire city opens up from the Panecillo viewpoint, with a statue of the winged Virgin Mary, the city’s patroness.

We head to the “Middle of the World” (the equator line).

There are two sites associated with the equator, and we will visit both:

1) Mitad del Mundo City.

Mitad del Mundo City is a tourist complex with a monument commemorating the geodetic expedition of 1736, which identified the equator line at this location. The “Middle of the World” complex belongs to the prefecture of Pichincha Province, Ecuador, and is in the parish of San Antonio in Quito’s metropolitan district, north of the city center.
Between 1979 and 1982, a 30 m monument was erected to mark what was believed to be the equator. A line extends from the center of the monument to represent the equator, and countless visitors have crossed it over the years. In fact, the entire structure stands 240 m south of the true line, whose position was correctly calculated in the twentieth century with the introduction of GPS positioning.

2) Intiñan Museum.

At this museum, we can try a series of demonstrations that the museum presents as connected with the equator line (swirling water, balancing a chicken egg, and walking along the equator). You will also learn about the cultures of ancient peoples, the “tsantsa” ritual, and see totems of various South American cultures. Traditional dwellings of cultures living in the country are on display, including a small house with belongings of an Indigenous family that lived here many generations ago.

Stops: Basilica del Voto Nacional, Main Square, “Golden Church,” San Francisco Square, hill with the Virgin Mary, Intiñan Museum and the “Middle of the World.”

## Rafain Grill Place and a Latin American Show

Rafain Grill Place is a huge air-conditioned restaurant with 1,200 seats and a parking area. Its menu is very varied, and you can try numerous meat dishes prepared from the freshest beef and pork. The buffet offers an abundance of vegetables, fruit and delicious desserts.

Lunch is accompanied by a show featuring Latin American performers presenting folk songs and modern dances. The restaurant visit takes place daily at 19:50. Pick-up is at your hotel.
